subject: geography
title: Tectonic Hazards Adventure: Processes
welcome_lead: Why do plates move? And how do volcanoes erupt? Today we look at the engine room.
meta_desc: GCSE Geography Tectonic Hazards processes — convection currents, subduction, volcanoes.
final_note: You learned the driving forces of plate movement and how volcanoes form.

concepts.def: Hot mantle rises, cools, sinks — drives plate movement
Denser oceanic plate sinks under continental plate
Molten rock beneath the Earth's surface
Molten rock once it reaches the surface
Steep cone — layered ash and lava — destructive margin
Wide gentle cone — runny lava — constructive margin

walkthroughs.body_html:
Deep inside Earth, heat from the core warms the mantle. Hot rock rises, cools near the crust, then sinks again.

These convection currents drag the plates above — the main driver of plate movement.

At destructive boundaries, the heavier oceanic plate sinks beneath the lighter continental plate.

The descending plate melts into magma. Pressure forces it up through cracks — creating violent composite volcanoes.

Composite (e.g. Mt Fuji): steep sides, sticky andesitic lava, violent eruptions — found at destructive margins.

Shield (e.g. Mauna Loa): gentle slopes, runny basaltic lava, frequent calm eruptions — found at constructive margins or hotspots.

mcqs.q: What process drives the movement of tectonic plates?
Which volcano type forms at DESTRUCTIVE margins?

numericals.q: Approximately how many active volcanoes are there on Earth today (whole numbers)?
numericals.hint: About one and a half thousand — a few erupt each year.

free_texts.q: What is the name for molten rock BELOW the Earth's surface? One word.
free_texts.hint: Once it reaches the surface it becomes lava.
